answer.exemplar: Eta squared is the between-groups share of the total variation, so 303.33 out of 333.33 is 0.91, and it does say that the three waiting-time groups account for nearly all of the spread in these fifteen numbers rather than for a technicality. What it cannot say is which pairs of means are responsible, that a 91 percent share would hold in a new sample, or that a waiting time matters to anyone; here the means are 14, 20, and 9 minutes, so the gap the study is built on is only 11 minutes even though the share is large. Treating a large share as a licence to act skips the step of asking whether an 11-minute difference is worth a policy change, and a proportion of variance is a statement about the sample, not about the size of the effect that matters.

questions.explanation: A strong response defines eta squared as the between-groups share of total variation, computes 303.33 / 333.33 = 0.91 for these fifteen times, notes that it says which share of the spread sits between the groups, and then separates that from the things it cannot settle, namely which pairs differ, whether the share repeats in a new sample, and whether an 11-minute gap between means of 9, 14, and 20 is worth acting on.
questions.hint: Ask how many minutes separate the lowest and highest group means.

questions.explanation: The test needs groups that are independent, measured the same way, and comparable apart from the schedule, and random assignment is what supplies all three at once while also balancing whatever noise the subject pool happens to carry. Letting doctors pick the schedule lets experience and caseload attach to the groups, and comparing against a historical average pits the new schedule against different subjects in a different era, so in both cases the schedule and everything else that moves with it vary together.

questions.explanation: The omnibus result established that the method means are not all equal, and the natural next question is which of them, which needs comparisons that were never made during the first analysis. With four means there are six pairs, and running all six at a 5 percent bar each would give roughly a 26 percent chance of at least one false positive, so the comparisons have to carry a correction for the family. Repeating the whole study or enlarging the best group adds data without answering the question the significant result actually raised.

questions.explanation: A fixed total of 120 buys the most power when it is spread evenly, because the within-groups mean square is an average of five variance estimates and averaging is most precise when every group contributes equally, while an uneven split throws away degrees of freedom on the group holding too few. Loading the first schedule with 60 subjects makes that group precise and the other four thin, and total sample size is already capped at 120, so adding subjects to a favourite group cannot buy back what the imbalance costs.

questions.explanation: The three averages of 14, 20, and 9 minutes are not all drawn from one population, and that is the whole content of the result, so a board can act on the fact that waiting times depend on which of the three routes produced them. It cannot act on which pair accounts for the gap, because the test named no pair, and it cannot treat the 20-minute group as the standard, because 20 is an average in this sample rather than a target anyone agreed to. Eta squared of 0.91 says 91 percent of the spread in these fifteen times sits between the groups, which is a statement about this sample and not a licence to move a service standard.
questions.hint: Ask which sentence would still be true if the three means had been permuted.
